summary: The English of 3:7–3:12 is mostly faithful and the commentary rulings are sound, but three renderings go against the normative commentators: 'gentle toward youth' in 3:12 (Bartenura and Rambam: composed, dignified), 'the sacred offerings' in 3:11 (Bartenura includes Temple property), and Rambam's 3:9 comment is misread (קניני הדעות are character traits, not knowledge). The main fault is the senses: many were filled mechanically or point to wrong homographs (רַבִּי as 'adj', הַבָּא as 'father', הַמַּלְבִּין as 'make bricks', תּוֹרָה as 'custom', קָם 'adversary', סָר 'low-spirited', אֵין 'where?'), and Hifil and Nifal verbs were given Qal senses; where the pack lists the right entry it is now set with lex. The model morphology needed fixes for נָתַנּוּ (1st plural), נִיר, בְּרַבִּי, לְבָבְךָ, אֵינוֹ and the four הֵימֶנּוּ, plus a few learner notes and the 3:7 apparatus.

value: אוֹמֵר is a participle: in Avot the attribution formula is 'X says', not a past tense.
תֶּן is the imperative of נתן: the first nun of the root drops in the imperative, as in biblical תֵּן; the segol of תֶּן is the short form before a closely joined word (Bartenura's heading has תֵּן).
שֶׁ is the Mishnaic relative; before the pronoun in שֶׁאַתָּה וְשֶׁלְּךָ שֶׁלּוֹ it is causal ('for you and yours are His'). שֶׁלּוֹ is the possessive 'of-him'.

The saying has two parts: a positive injunction (Rabbi Elazar of Bartota) and a verse from Chronicles that supports it. Rabbi Shimon's saying is a separate sentence; the long participial subject is resumed by מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו.
הַמְהַלֵּךְ is a Piel participle; שׁוֹנֶה, מַפְסִיק and אוֹמֵר are participles that continue the subject. The subject hangs until the main verb מַעֲלֶה.
מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ: the Hitpael participle of חיב, 'be held liable'; the idiom means to be liable to forfeit his life.
patches.reason: The note on תֶּן was wrong: the loss of the nun in the imperative of נתן is not Mishnaic or late; biblical Hebrew already has תֵּן. Other notes unchanged.

patches.value: Rabbi Dostai son of Rabbi Yannai, in the name of Rabbi Meir, says: Whoever forgets a single thing from his learning, Scripture accounts it to him as if he were forfeiting his life, as it is said: “Only take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the things that your eyes saw.” One might think this holds even if his learning was too hard for him; the teaching says: “and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life.” Thus he is not forfeiting his life until he sits and removes them from his heart.
patches.reason: 'Too hard for him' is Bartenura's sense (קָשָׁה עָלָיו) more exactly than 'too strong'; ', in the same passage' rendered the printed citation (שם), which the translation otherwise leaves untranslated, like (דברים ד).

patches.value: 'Learning' translates מִשְׁנָה in its general sense of what has been repeated and learned, not the book 'Mishnah'. 'Forfeiting his life' renders מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ, literally 'liable in his soul'. 'Too hard for him' is Bartenura's reading of תָּקְפָה עָלָיו: it was hard for him and he forgot it because of the difficulty. The two readings of why forgetting counts against him are recorded under the Bartenura anchor. The printed citations (דברים ד) and (שם) are not translated.

patches.value: Rambam: the philosophers also agree that when the habit of the virtues comes first and becomes a firm possession, and only afterward he learns wisdom, which spurs him on to those good things, it adds joy and love of wisdom; but when (other) traits of character (קניני הדעות) are acquired first and only then he learns, so that wisdom restrains him from what he has grown used to craving, wisdom grows heavy for him and he abandons it.
patches.reason: קניני הדעות here are acquired dispositions of character (Rambam's דעות), the counterpart of the habit of virtues; they are not 'knowledge'. The summary reversed the point: it is bad habit, not learning, that comes first in the second case.

Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative) reads the first pair as about intention: one who strives to know wisdom in order to guard himself from sin keeps it. On 'deeds exceed wisdom' he asks how deeds can exceed knowledge, and answers that one who undertakes beforehand to do whatever the sages will teach him is credited as if he had done it, citing 'we will do and we will hear' (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 22).

value: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר 'He used to say' continues Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's sayings from 3:9. The pair of sayings is built on כָּל שֶׁ... 'anyone whose/with whom'.

נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ: נוֹחָה is a feminine participle (agreeing with רוּחַ, which is here feminine); הֵימֶנּוּ is the Mishnaic form of מִמֶּנּוּ, 'from him'. The idiom is 'the spirit is at ease with him'.
The two halves are parallel. Bartenura reads the first as a sign, not a cause: whoever is loved below is known (בְּיָדוּעַ) to be loved above. אֵין negates each half.

Rabbi Dosa's list has four items joined by וְ: two use the genitive particle שֶׁל (שֵׁנָה שֶׁל שַׁחֲרִית 'sleep of morning', יַיִן שֶׁל צָהֳרַיִם 'wine of noon') and two are construct chains (שִׂיחַת הַיְלָדִים, יְשִׁיבַת בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת); the plural participle מוֹצִיאִין has the whole list as subject.
עַם הָאָרֶץ is literally 'people of the land'; in the Mishnah it means an unlearned person, a person ignorant of Torah. הַמָּקוֹם is literally 'the Place', a name of God.
patches.reason: Two notes were wrong: the items with שֶׁל are not construct chains, and Bartenura's בְּיָדוּעַ makes the first saying a sign, not 'cause and effect'.
Bartenura counts both the offerings of the altar and the property consecrated to the upkeep of the Temple (קָדְשֵׁי בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת); 'offerings' leaves out the second.
מְבַזֶּה is Piel; sense 1.1 is the Qal. The entry has no Piel sense, so the general heading 1 is the right one.

patches.value: 'Brazenly flouts the Torah' renders הַמְגַלֶּה פָנִים בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא כַהֲלָכָה. Rambam, Rabbeinu Yonah and Bartenura's second explanation take the idiom as acting shamelessly, in the open, against the Torah. Bartenura's first explanation, one who 'shows faces' (explanations) in the Torah that are not according to halakha, is recorded under the Bartenura anchor. 'The sacred things' renders הַקָּדָשִׁים: Bartenura includes both the offerings of the altar and property consecrated to the Temple's upkeep. 'The covenant of Abraham' is circumcision; Bartenura takes the offence as one who was not circumcised, or who was circumcised and draws the foreskin forward to hide it; Rabbeinu Yonah names only the second. 'The festivals' is Bartenura's reading, the intermediate days (חוֹל הַמּוֹעֵד).
patches.reason: The note gave only the second of Bartenura's two cases for הַמֵּפֵר בְּרִיתוֹ, and did not explain 'sacred things'.

patches.value: Rabbi Yishmael says: Be yielding to a superior, and composed with the young, and receive every person with joy.
patches.reason: Bartenura and Rambam agree that נוֹחַ לְתִשְׁחֹרֶת means: before a young man do not make yourself light, but stand calmly and with composure, keeping your dignity. 'Gentle toward youth' says something else (kindness to the young).

patches.value: 'Yielding to a superior' renders קַל לְרֹאשׁ. Bartenura and Rambam both read it as being quick to serve a person of standing; the English keeps the idiom without expanding it. 'Composed with the young' renders נוֹחַ לְתִשְׁחֹרֶת; Bartenura and Rambam: do not make yourself light with the young but stand before them calmly and with dignity, and yet receive everyone cheerfully. 'Receive' is the plain sense of מְקַבֵּל; Bartenura also derives it from the Aramaic קֳבֵל 'facing', so 'meet'. Bartenura's alternative reading (youth and old age with the Creator) is recorded under his anchor.
patches.reason: Brought in line with the corrected English.

value: הֱוֵי is the Mishnaic imperative of הָיָה ('be'); וֶהֱוֵי is the same with the conjunction, the vowel pattern of the conjunction before a guttural.
הֱוֵי קַל לְרֹאשׁ: the predicate adjective with ל. קַל is 'light'; Rambam says its sense is known, 'lightness'; the figure is of a person who does not weigh on a superior, who is quick to serve.

נוֹחַ is used as an adjective, 'easy, at rest, composed' (Rambam: הַיִּשּׁוּב וְהַהֲנָחָה); תִּשְׁחֹרֶת is a rare noun from the root שחר 'black', for 'youth', the time of black hair (Bartenura, Rambam). Rabbeinu Yonah derives it differently: from שחוור, a lord or official, or from the Targum's שחרית 'forced service' (Num 16:15).
מְקַבֵּל is the Piel participle of קבל, 'to receive'. With הֱוֵי it forms a periphrastic imperative, 'be one who receives'.

The sentence is three clauses of the pattern 'be + adjective/participle'. The last sets the general rule for every person (אֶת כָּל הָאָדָם), after two specific cases of an older and a younger person.
patches.reason: The note claimed תִּשְׁחֹרֶת is 'Aramaic-influenced in form' on Rabbeinu Yonah's authority; Rabbeinu Yonah cites the Targum for a different meaning (an official, or forced service), not for the form.

value: Spelling: Vilna reads לתשחורת for לְתִשְׁחֹרֶת.
Bartenura's alternative explanation (the first two clauses are about one's own youth and old age toward the Creator) is recorded under his anchor and not adopted.

Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative) reads קַל לְרֹאשׁ as making oneself light before a chief or lord; he does not take תִּשְׁחֹרֶת as 'youth' but as an official (from שחוור, 'lord'), to whom one should be pleasant in speech, or, from the Targum's שחרית in Num 16:15, as service: be easy in serving a great man and doing his will.
patches.reason: The old line did not record Rabbeinu Yonah's different sense of תִּשְׁחֹרֶת, a real alternative to 'youth'.
נָתַנּוּ is 1st common plural, 'we gave' (the נ of the root assimilated to the ending ־נוּ); the 3rd plural is נָתְנוּ.
The word is נִיר 'tilled ground, furrow' (Bartenura, citing Jer 4:3), not נֵר 'lamp'; root ניר.
יָד is a primary noun with no verbal root; ידה ('throw, praise') is a different root.

patches.reason: בְּרַבִּי is contracted from בַּר רַבִּי: the first element is Aramaic בַּר 'son', not Hebrew בֶּן, and has no root בנה.
לְבָבְךָ is from לֵבָב, the long form of 'heart', not לֵב.
אֵינוֹ is אֵין with the 3rd masculine singular suffix ('he is not'); the suffix must be split off.
